distinguishing_features: Actively re-stresses the gasket via a pneumatic bladder actuator, rather than only inferring/monitoring a leak from existing signals (closed-loop actuation vs. passive diagnosis)
Uses exhaust flow rate as the primary actuation signal to drive a physical seal-pressure change, not merely as a diagnostic proxy
Adds new hardware (bladder, solenoid valve, MCU) to modulate contact pressure in real time, whereas prior art uses zero new hardware and software analytics
parsed.objective_technical_problem: How to actively maintain sufficient gasket contact pressure to suppress outgassing/permeation-driven leak-rate drift during high-flow, high-vacuum operation, rather than only detecting or predicting an incipient leak.
parsed.viable_reason: The stated physics is internally inconsistent and implausible: exhaust flow rate cannot servce as a pressure actuator signal to 're-stress' the gasket to compensate outgassing, higher flow-induced convective cooling would reduce not raise permeation flux in a way the loop could correct, and the claimed 5%->1% drift reduction by gas-flow-coupled bladder pressurization is not demonstrably achievable at the stated scale.
parsed.non_obvious_reason: Closed-loop pneumatic re-stressing of a vacuum gasket driven by exhaust flow rate is a genuine mechanism departure from the passive monitoring approaches of the prior art, not a routine parameter change.
